title: Six Hundred Trees in the Ground: What Our First Planting Season Taught Us
body:
We planted 600 trees across one hectare of degraded land in our foundation year. Here is what went right, what went wrong, and what we are doing differently in season two.

The work began in early 2025. Our team of ten identified a site showing the characteristic markers of degraded Sahelian landscape: compacted topsoil, sparse groundcover, erosion channels cutting through what had once been productive farmland. The community had been watching the land deteriorate for years. What was once a reliable source of food and shade had become a dusty expanse that flooded in the rains and baked in the dry season.

We started with the soil. Before a single seedling went in, our ecologists were on their knees reading the ground — assessing organic matter levels, identifying compaction layers, documenting which areas held moisture and which shed it immediately after rain. This is the part that never makes the press release. The part that makes or breaks the planting. Without understanding the soil, you are guessing. And guessing, at scale, is expensive failure.

The species mix was community-validated. We worked with elders and farmers to identify which trees they remembered from the landscape before degradation — which ones had provided shade, fodder, fruit, timber, or medicine. Then we cross-referenced that knowledge with ecological literature and our field observations. The final mix was native, functional, and meaningful to the people who would live with it. We selected species adapted to the local rainfall pattern and soil chemistry, prioritizing those with multiple uses to the community.

Six hundred trees went in over several weeks. Each one was planted with a water-retaining basin, mulched with locally sourced organic material, and tagged for monitoring. We established a watering schedule for the first dry season and recruited community members to serve as tree guardians — each responsible for a section of the planting site.

What went right: community ownership was real. Several families adopted individual trees — checking on them, reporting irrigation needs, keeping goats away from the young growth. This is exactly what we had hoped to build. When a community sees trees not as someone else's project but as their own investment in the future, survival rates improve dramatically. We also saw children taking interest, which tells us the educational dimension of the work is landing.

What went wrong: logistics proved more challenging than anticipated. Transporting seedlings to the site without damage required more careful planning than we had allocated. Some seedlings arrived stressed and took longer to establish. We also underestimated the intensity of termite pressure in certain sections of the site, losing several trees before we implemented protective measures. These are the lessons that textbooks do not teach — they come only from doing the work.

We have adjusted our planting protocol for season two. Seedlings will be hardened at a staging nursery closer to the site before planting. We are introducing termite-resistant mulch barriers. And we are expanding the community guardian program based on the model that worked in season one.

The hectare is not a forest yet. But it is a start. The soil is already responding — we have documented measurable improvements in moisture retention in the planted areas compared to adjacent unplanted control plots. Season two begins soon, and we are carrying forward every lesson from the first.

title: What Bush Burning Does to Topsoil: A Conversation with Our Field Teams
body:
The damage from a single season of bush burning can take years to reverse. Our ecologists explain what happens under the surface and why sensitization is as important as planting.

Every year across the Sahel and Nigeria's savannah belt, farmers burn their fields after harvest. The reasons are understandable: it clears the debris of the previous season quickly, it kills some pests, and it has been done this way for generations. The practice feels efficient, and when your neighbours are all doing it, there is strong social pressure to follow. But the problem is what it does below the surface — damage that is invisible but devastating.

A healthy topsoil is not just dirt. It is a living system — billions of microorganisms, fungal networks, invertebrates, plant roots and their decay. It is this living system that holds water, cycles nutrients, and gives crops their yield. A teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms than there are people on Earth. These organisms break down organic matter into forms that plant roots can absorb. They create channels that allow water to infiltrate rather than run off. They are, in every meaningful sense, the engine of agricultural productivity.

When you burn, you kill it. The temperatures reached during a bush fire — often exceeding 400°C at the surface — sterilize the top layer of soil. You also volatilize the nitrogen that took years to accumulate, sending it into the atmosphere as gas rather than keeping it available for the next crop. You cook the organic matter that gave the soil its structure, turning it to ash that blows away or washes off in the first rain. And you leave a surface that, bare and hardened, sheds the next rainfall rather than absorbing it.

The water that runs off carries the ash and whatever nutrients remain, depositing them in rivers and streams where they cause their own problems. Meanwhile, the field that was burned sits exposed to the sun, baking harder, cracking, losing the capillary structure that would have drawn moisture upward to plant roots during the dry season.

One season of burning can set a topsoil back by years. Multiple seasons of burning, compounded by overgrazing and without organic matter inputs, can make land effectively dead — unable to support the crops, trees, or ground cover that would allow it to recover. This is desertification in slow motion. And it is happening across millions of hectares.

This is not a lecture. It is biology. And our sensitization work starts from that biology, not from a moral position. We have learned that telling people they are wrong achieves nothing. Showing them what is happening in their own soil achieves everything.

When we sit with farmers in our program communities, we do not tell them bush burning is wrong. We show them what their soil contains before and after burning. We bring a simple soil sampling kit and demonstrate the difference in organic matter, in moisture content, in the presence of earthworms and other soil fauna. We discuss the economics: what does yield loss cost over five years? What does buying fertilizer to replace what burning destroyed cost compared to simply not burning?

We talk about alternatives — composting, mulching, controlled management, cover cropping — that achieve the same agricultural goals without the long-term damage. These are not theoretical alternatives. They are practices being used successfully by farmers in similar environments across West Africa. We connect farmers with peers who have made the transition and can speak from experience.

The conversation is difficult. Changing a practice that feels like tradition always is. But it is the conversation that makes the planting work. Because if we plant trees on land that continues to be burned, we are running on a treadmill. The restoration only sticks if the practices that caused the degradation change alongside it.

title: Urban Trees in Lagos: Why City Greening is Climate Action
body:
Africa's fastest-growing cities are losing green cover just as they need it most. We make the case for urban greening as a serious climate intervention, not just beautification.

Lagos, Abuja, Kano, Port Harcourt — Nigeria's cities are expanding at a speed that outpaces planning. Roads are laid over wetlands, markets sprawl into floodplains, and trees are felled for construction timber or simply to make way for development. In the process, the green infrastructure that once tempered urban heat, absorbed stormwater, and filtered air is disappearing. And the consequences are felt most acutely by the people who can least afford alternatives.

This matters more than aesthetics. The data is unambiguous. Urban trees reduce ambient temperatures by 2–8°C through shade and evapotranspiration. In a city like Lagos, where dry-season temperatures regularly exceed 35°C and where millions of people work outdoors, this is not a comfort issue — it is a survival issue. Heat-related illness, reduced labour productivity, and increased energy costs for cooling are all direct consequences of urban heat islands, and all are mitigated by tree cover.

Trees absorb particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide — pollutants that cause respiratory disease, cardiovascular problems, and premature death. In Nigerian cities where traffic congestion is severe and vehicle emission standards are minimal, street trees function as a first line of respiratory defense. Studies in comparable tropical cities have shown that tree-lined streets have measurably lower concentrations of harmful particulates than treeless ones.

They slow stormwater runoff, reducing flood risk. Lagos floods regularly, and the floods are getting worse. While many factors contribute — including poor drainage infrastructure and development in flood-prone areas — the loss of permeable, vegetated surfaces is a significant one. Trees and their root systems absorb rainfall, slow surface flow, and reduce the volume of water that overwhelms drainage systems. A mature tree can intercept thousands of litres of rainfall per year.

In cities where millions walk, cycle, or work outdoors, these are not luxuries — they are public health infrastructure. Urban greening is climate adaptation in its most practical, immediate, and cost-effective form.

Our Urban Greening program starts from this evidence base. We work with municipal authorities and community groups to identify high-impact planting sites — school compounds, market perimeters, roadside corridors, community spaces, and places of worship — and plant species selected for urban resilience: drought tolerance, pollution resistance, rapid canopy development, and non-invasive root systems that will not damage infrastructure.

The work is different from rural restoration. The soil is often compacted, contaminated with construction debris, or underlain by concrete and pipes. The politics are more complex — every piece of urban land has competing claims. The maintenance challenge is real — a tree in a city needs protection from construction, vehicle damage, and vandalism in ways a rural tree does not. It needs watering during establishment in environments where there is no natural irrigation.

But the impact per tree is arguably higher. A single mature tree in a dense urban neighborhood serves thousands of people every day. Its shade cools a market. Its canopy filters the air a school breathes. Its roots slow the flood that would otherwise enter homes. When we think about where trees deliver the most benefit per unit of investment, cities — especially fast-growing African cities — are near the top of the list.

We are beginning with pilot projects in three Nigerian cities. The results will inform a scalable model that we intend to offer to municipal governments across the region. Urban greening is not a substitute for systemic climate action. But it is one of the few interventions that delivers measurable benefits within years, not decades.
excerpt: Africa's fastest-growing cities are losing green cover just as they need it most. We make the case for urban greening as a serious climate intervention, not just beautification.

title: A Farmer's Perspective: Why We Stopped Burning Our Fields
body:
One farmer from our first program community explains the conversation that changed how he manages land — and what made the difference between lecture and dialogue.

"I have been farming this land for thirty years. My father farmed it before me, and his father before him. We always burned after harvest — everyone did. It was the way you prepared the ground for the next season. You burned, the ash settled, and you planted into it. Nobody told us it was a problem. Or if they did, they told us like we were stupid, and we stopped listening."

"Government people came sometimes. They would stand in front of us with their fine clothes and tell us bush burning was bad. But they never showed us why. They never got their hands dirty. They never asked us what we thought or what we had observed. They talked at us, and then they left. And we kept burning, because it was what we knew."

"When the Foundation people came, they were different. They did not lecture. They asked questions first. They sat with us under the trees — what trees we had left — and they asked what we remembered about the soil when we were young. Was it darker? Did it hold water longer? Did the crops grow taller? And we said yes, yes, it was different then. The soil was softer. Richer. You could smell it after rain — that good, dark smell. Now it smells like dust."

"Then they showed us why. They dug small holes — here and there in the field — and showed us what was in the soil. The worms, the tiny roots, the dark matter that holds everything together. And then they dug holes in a section that had just been burned. The difference was there for anyone to see. The burned soil was lighter. Harder. Empty. No worms. No roots. Just ash and clay."

"That is when I understood. Not because someone told me I was wrong, but because I could see it with my own eyes. The soil I had been burning every year was dying. And I was the one killing it."

"The change was not easy. We still clear the fields after harvest — you have to, or you cannot plant. But now we cut and pile instead of burning. We let the stalks and leaves rot where they fall, or we gather them into compost heaps. It is more work, yes. My wife says I complain about it every season. But the soil is already changing. After just two seasons of not burning, the topsoil is darker. It holds water longer after rain. I had more earthworms this year than I have seen in a decade."

"My neighbor noticed it too. He came to my field after the rains and said the ground looked different — better. He asked me what I was doing differently. I told him. He is trying it this season."

"That conversation — farmer to farmer — is how this spreads. Not from a pamphlet. Not from a government announcement. From one farmer looking at another farmer's field and seeing the difference. From the ground."

"I tell the Foundation people: keep bringing farmers to see. Keep digging those holes. Keep asking questions instead of giving lectures. That is what works. That is what changed my mind. And if it changed mine, it can change anyone's."
excerpt: One farmer from our first program community explains the conversation that changed how he manages land — and what made the difference between lecture and dialogue.

title: Why Climate & Green World Foundation Exists: A Note from Dr. Anosike
body:
I spent years watching the landscapes I loved shrink. Here is why I decided a lone voice was no longer enough.

For as long as I can remember, I have been drawn to the natural world. As a child in southeastern Nigeria, the forests and waterways were not scenery — they were the context of daily life. We swam in clean rivers. We walked through forests that seemed permanent, where the canopy was so dense that rain reached you minutes after it started. The air smelled of green things growing. Seasons were reliable. The land provided.

Over the decades, I watched that world shrink. Not suddenly — not in the dramatic way that makes international news — but steadily, persistently, in ways that only someone paying attention would notice. A patch of forest cleared for a road that was never completed. A stream that ran clear in my childhood turning brown, then orange, then dead. Fields that had fed families for generations producing less each year, until they were abandoned.

The causes were not mysterious. Deforestation for timber and development. Bush burning that destroyed topsoil fertility. Oil spills and illegal refining that poisoned water systems. A growing population placing demands on ecosystems that were already under stress. And underneath it all, a changing climate — shifting rainfall patterns, intensifying heat, making everything harder for the people and landscapes already on the edge.

I spent years doing what I could as an individual. Planting trees on my own land and on any land where I could get permission. Speaking to community groups about soil health and bush burning alternatives. Writing to newspapers about the environmental degradation I was witnessing. Contributing to local reforestation initiatives wherever I found them.

But individual action, however sincere, has limits. I could plant a hundred trees, but my neighbor's unmanaged land would erode into my plot. I could explain the science of soil degradation to one community, but the same conversation needed to happen in thousands of communities. The scale of the problem demanded an institutional response — coordinated, funded, measured, and sustained over years and decades, not dependent on any one person's energy or lifespan.

That is why Climate & Green World Foundation exists. Not as another NGO adding to the noise — Nigeria has many organizations with environmental mandates, and some do excellent work. But too many operate without rigor, without measurement, without the honesty to report what has failed alongside what has succeeded. We aim to be different.

Our mandate is specific: restore degraded landscapes, defend ecosystems from pollution, and equip communities to thrive in a changing climate. Our geography is focused: we start in Nigeria and the Sahel, where we know the land, the people, the politics, and the ecology. We will expand only when we have earned the right to, by demonstrating results where we began.

We are small. We are honest about that. In our first year we planted 600 trees across one hectare. That is not a headline-grabbing number. It will not appear in any ranking of the world's largest reforestation efforts. But every one of those trees is in the ground, monitored, and cared for. Every one represents a conversation with a community, a choice of species based on evidence, a commitment to follow through for years, not months.

Our approach is built on five principles. First, we are evidence-led: we measure what we do, report honestly, and adjust based on data. Second, we are community-rooted: no project proceeds without community engagement, validation, and ownership. Third, we plant native species selected for ecological function, not for speed of growth or ease of sourcing. Fourth, we think in decades, not quarters — landscape restoration is slow work, and we are structured for the long term. Fifth, we are accountable: our governance, our finances, and our outcomes are transparent.

The work is slow. Restoration always is. A degraded hectare does not become a healthy landscape in a year, or even in five. The soil must rebuild its microbial communities. The trees must establish root systems deep enough to survive dry seasons. The community must develop the practices and institutions to maintain what has been planted. This takes time, patience, and sustained investment.

But it is real. And it will grow. Every hectare restored teaches us something. Every community conversation deepens our understanding. Every season in the field refines our methods. We are building something that will outlast any of us — a foundation in the truest sense of the word.

I invite you to join us. Not because the work is glamorous — it is not. Not because the results are instant — they are not. But because the alternative is to watch, and I have done enough watching.
excerpt: I spent years watching the landscapes I loved shrink. Here is why I decided a lone voice was no longer enough.

title: Climate & Green World Foundation Registered with CAC Nigeria
body:
We are pleased to announce the formal registration of Climate & Green World Foundation with the Corporate Affairs Commission of Nigeria.

This registration marks a significant milestone in our journey from an individual vision to an institutional reality. After months of preparation, documentation, and review, the Climate & Green World Foundation is now a legally recognized entity under Nigerian law, empowered to enter partnerships, receive funding, employ staff, and operate programs across the country.

The Foundation was established with a clear mandate: to restore degraded landscapes, defend ecosystems from pollution, and equip communities to thrive in a changing climate. Our initial focus is on Nigeria and the Sahel region, with a long-term vision of expanding our work across the African continent as our capacity and track record grow.

Registration with the CAC is not just a legal formality. It represents accountability. It means our operations, finances, and governance are subject to regulatory oversight. It means our partners — corporate, governmental, and individual — can engage with us through established legal frameworks with confidence that their contributions are managed responsibly and directed toward our stated mission.

The registration also enables us to pursue partnerships and funding opportunities that require formal legal status. Many international development agencies, corporate social responsibility programs, and philanthropic foundations require their implementing partners to be registered legal entities with proper governance structures. This registration opens those doors.

Our governance structure includes a Board of Directors with expertise spanning ecology, community development, finance, and law. The Board provides strategic oversight and ensures that the Foundation's activities remain aligned with our mission and values. Day-to-day operations are managed by our Executive Director and a small but dedicated team.

We extend our gratitude to Dr. Ike Anosike, whose vision, persistence, and years of individual environmental advocacy laid the groundwork for this institution. We also thank the legal professionals who guided us through the registration process and the early supporters who believed in this work before it had a name or a formal structure.

The Foundation is now open to partnership inquiries, funding applications, and volunteer engagement. We invite organizations and individuals who share our commitment to ecological restoration and community-centered climate action to reach out. Whether you are a corporation seeking a credible environmental partner, a government agency looking for a delivery organization, or an individual who wants to contribute to meaningful work — there is a place for you here.

Contact us at info@climategreenworld.org or visit our website at climategreenworld.org to learn more about our programs, our approach, and how you can get involved.
excerpt: We are pleased to announce the formal registration of Climate & Green World Foundation with the Corporate Affairs Commission of Nigeria.
